Failed sections exhibited higher optimum moisture content (22.81%) and lower maximum dry density (1.67 Mg/m³) compared to unfailed sections (17.05% and 1.73 Mg/m³). Permeability values were 8.42 × 10⁻⁶ m/s and 5.30 × 10⁻⁶ m/s, respectively. Shear strength parameters indicated cohesion of 24.73 kPa and friction angle of 28° for failed sections, and 18.97 kPa and 37° for unfailed sections. Seepage and slope stability analyses using GeoSlope, 2007 yielded seepage discharges between 2.87–3.29 m³/day/km (failed) and 1.35–3.15 m³/day/km (unfailed). Factors of safety for upstream slopes were 2.50 and 3.08, and for downstream slopes 1.97 and 2.39, respectively. A survey of 100 downstream households revealed significant socio-economic impacts, with 87% reporting high flood intensity, loss of livelihoods, reduced irrigation, and decline in fishing activities. Pearson correlation analysis (r < 0.5, p < 0.01) confirmed a significant relationship between dam failure and socio-economic variables. The study highlights seepage as a key factor in embankment performance and underscores the need for improved seepage control and monitoring to ensure long-term dam safety.

Existing deep learning models exhibit limited accuracy in predicting dam displacement deformation due to their inability to effectively distinguish noise from genuine signals. To this end, this paper proposes a method for predicting dam displacement deformation based on the variational modal decomposition-long short-term memory-Optuna (VMD-LSTM-Optuna) model. This method uses variational modal decomposition (VMD) and cross-correlation analysis as pre-prediction denoising modules to extract genuine structural responses from raw monitoring data. Subsequently, long short-term memory (LSTM) optimised using the Optuna algorithm performs time-series forecasting on the cleaned data. To validate the predictive capability of the model, an engineering case study was conducted. The results demonstrate that the proposed method can forecast future displacement trends more accurately than other models, proving its reliability in providing real-time early warnings for dam safety.

Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.

Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.

High arch dams are complex structures subjected to strong nonlinear behavior and extreme loading conditions, where achieving high-accuracy prediction of real-time full-field structural physical states remains challenging due to sparse monitoring data and insufficient guidance for sensor placement. To address this issue, this study proposes a sensor perception optimization-driven digital twin framework that integrates numerical simulation with deep transfer learning. To improve sensor layout design, modal observability is adopted to evaluate the sensitivity of monitoring points to structural responses, while the condition number is used to assess reconstruction stability. In addition, a hybrid optimization strategy combining orthogonal triangular decomposition for candidate sensor screening and greedy iterative selection for layout refinement is developed to integrate heterogeneous monitoring technologies. A case study of a prototype high arch dam under normal, extreme, and seismic conditions demonstrates that the proposed method significantly improves the reconstruction accuracy of deformation and stress fields, enhances sensing robustness, and effectively captures nonlinear and damage-evolving structural behaviors. The proposed framework shows strong potential for intelligent monitoring and safety assessment of high arch dams.

Hydropower plants heavily depend on the performance of turbine generators, where unexpected equipment failure can cause downtime, loss, and even safety issues in the process. The traditional condition monitoring methods mainly focus on vibration signals detected by a single sensor, which is not integrated with multiple sources and lacks the ability to perceive the risk at the plant level. In addition, the majority of the studies do not consider the equipment level health condition and structural risk factors to develop unified decision support for safety issues. To address the issues, the paper proposes a framework for the integrated health assessment and safety early warning framework, which is developed by integrating the equipment level fault diagnosis model based on the CNN-LSTM network and the structural risk assessment model developed by the GloHydroRes dataset. The novelty of the proposed multi-level data fusion framework integrates equipment-level and plant-level information for safety assessment that incorporates multi-channel vibration and torque signals along with structural attributes such as dam height, reservoir volume, and installed capacity to derive a unified safety risk index. Experimental validation using the proposed approach on the SEU multi-sensor dataset achieved high classification performance with Accuracy of 0.9634, Precision of 0.8642, Recall of 0.9613, F1-score of 0.9065, and MCC of 0.8662. Moreover, multi-class ROC analysis indicated high performance with AUC values of 0.9936 (Low Risk), 0.9930 (Medium Risk), and 0.9997 (High Risk), outperforming individual CNN, LSTM, and Random Forest approaches. The unified safety index revealed that 46.6% of samples were classified as Low Risk, 34.1% of samples were classified as Medium Risk, and 19.3% of samples were classified as High Risk, thus validating the efficacy of the proposed decision support mechanism. Compared with traditional fault detection methods, the proposed approach improves the reliability of fault prediction results, reduces false alarm rates, and enables proactive maintenance decisions based on risk considerations.

Water level monitoring of rivers, water reservoirs, and dams plays an important role in flood prediction, water resource management, and environmental safety. The conventional water level monitoring techniques include manual observation and sensor-based techniques. The conventional image-based and deep learning-based water level measurement techniques have improved accuracy of the water level measurement system. The dataset used in this research work is the Water Gauge Computer Vision Dataset available in Roboflow Universe, which consists of about 500 real-world water gauge images taken under varying environmental conditions. The proposed water level measurement system differs from the conventional techniques in terms of the usage of YOLOv8-based gauge region detection, hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for digit detection, and classical computer vision techniques like edge detection and Hough transform for accurate waterline detection. The experimental results show high detection accuracy with Precision 0.960, Recall 0.955, F1-score 0.958, Accuracy 0.969, and mAP 0.970. The system has high estimation accuracy as well, as shown by MAE 0.036 m, RMSE 0.081 m and MAPE 3.55%, which shows minimal prediction error in the results.

The 21st century has emerged as a transformative period for dam engineering, shaped by rapid technological innovation, increasing environmental awareness, the aging of existing infrastructure, and the growing global need for climate resilience. As demands for water resources, renewable energy, and sustainable infrastructure continue to intensify, the role of dams has expanded far beyond their traditional purposes. Today, dams function not only as vital components of critical infrastructure but also as platforms for innovation, sustainability, and adaptive design and maintenance. In this Reprint, the editorial article “Advances in Dam Engineering of the 21st Century” highlights major developments across a broad range of dam engineering disciplines in the first quarter of the century. It provides an integrated overview of progress in materials science, design methodologies, construction practices, monitoring technologies, and comprehensive risk management strategies, and it examines the digital transformation that is reshaping the field. The twelve papers included in this Reprint present a cohesive and detailed portrait of contemporary dam engineering. Collectively, they encompass advanced modeling, risk assessment, material behavior, and safety governance, outlining the modern pipeline of dam safety practice, from hazard definition and structural modeling to material testing and policy evolution.

Accurately predicting dam slope displacement is a crucial prerequisite for ensuring the operational safety of hydraulic structures and preventing potential landslide disasters. However, existing prediction methods remain inadequate in the collaborative realization of temporal feature representation and high-precision regression, and their performance is especially limited under conditions of high dimensionality, noise interference, and small sample sizes. To address this issue, this paper proposes a hybrid prediction model that integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and an AdaBoost-enhanced Relevance Vector Machine (RVM). First, the displacement time series is reconstructed via a sliding window to construct feature samples suitable for CNN input, thereby extracting local correlation structures and multi-scale features from the time series. Subsequently, the extracted features are fed into the AdaBoost–RVM model for regression prediction, so as to improve the prediction accuracy and generalization capability. The model is validated using monitoring data from a dam slope. The results demonstrate that, compared with various benchmark models, the proposed method achieves superior performance in terms of MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and R², and can well capture the displacement variation trend with stable predictions. The proposed method can provide an effective approach for the deformation analysis of dam slopes.

Missing data is inevitable in dam monitoring systems and poses significant challenges to dam safety monitoring and early warning. Such missing values typically manifest in either discrete or continuous patterns. However, conventional imputation methods are often inadequate for scenarios in which both discrete and continuous missing patterns occur together within structural responses, particularly when external environmental covariates, such as reservoir water level and air temperature, are also unavailable. To address this limitation, a hybrid unsupervised framework called hierarchical clustering-assisted probabilistic principal component analysis is proposed. Within this framework, Ward’s hierarchical clustering is first applied to discern latent spatiotemporal patterns and facilitate adaptive clustering of monitoring variables. Subsequently, probabilistic principal component analysis models are constructed within each cluster to enable probabilistic reconstruction of both discrete and continuous missing entries. Benefiting from its probabilistic latent variable formulation, the method not only yields accurate point estimates but also quantifies residual noise uncertainty through the estimated isotropic variance, thereby providing a measure of estimation reliability. The proposed method was systematically validated using incomplete radial deformation monitoring data from an arch dam across four representative scenarios that combine varying discrete missing ratios with continuous block gaps. The results show that the proposed method consistently outperforms benchmark techniques in reconstruction accuracy and pattern preservation. Without requiring external environmental data, the framework offers a reliable solution for dam safety monitoring data reconstruction, supporting structural condition assessment and safety management.

Fragmented safety-monitoring data across the dam construction lifecycle hinder reliable digital twins and automated asset management. This paper examines how such information can be exchanged automatically and semantically across heterogeneous systems using open industry standards. An automated openBIM-enabled framework is developed by integrating digital-twin information modelling with Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) and the Smart Applications REFerence ontology. A case study of an ultra-high arch dam validates the structured and traceable exchange of safety-monitoring information for digital twin applications. The results are important for owners and contractors because standards-based information continuity strengthens semantic consistency and interoperability in safety-monitoring processes. The framework provides a practical basis for future open-standard digital twins and further automation of construction lifecycle management systems.

Reservoir-related disasters have become increasingly frequent in recent years due to abnormal climate phenomena, including heavy rainfall and droughts, driven by rapid climate change.As similar risks are also rising in South Korea, time-series observations were conducted in areas surrounding reservoirs using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite data, which are relatively unaffected by weather conditions and daynight constraints.In this study, 57 Sentinel-1 SAR images acquired between October 2023 and October 2025 were used to perform time-series interferometric analysis of the dam structure and surrounding areas of Geumgwang Reservoir in Anseong, Gyeonggi-do, South Korea.Two algorithms were employed: the small baseline subset method, which constructs interferometric networks from image pairs with short spatial and temporal baselines for time-series analysis, and the persistent scatterer interferometry method, which extracts persistent scatterers with stable backscattering characteristics and analyzes their temporal evolution.The results derived from both techniques were compared at four locations, and all sites showed relatively stable deformation signals.The strong agreement between the two interferometric approaches further confirms the reliability of the processed dataset.Consequently, the dataset can serve as a reliable reference for long-term safety monitoring and various secondary applications.

To ensure the structural safety of concrete dams and prevent temperature-induced cracking, finite element methods are commonly used to simulate temperature and stress fields. The accuracy of finite element simulation strongly depends on the reliability of thermodynamic parameters. Parameters obtained from conventional laboratory tests cannot fully represent complex in situ conditions. They are affected by ambient temperature fluctuations, cooling water circulation, and insulation measures. Therefore, thermodynamic parameter inversion based on field monitoring data is necessary to improve the accuracy and reliability of temperature control analysis. To address slow convergence, local stagnation, and limited accuracy of traditional intelligent optimization algorithms, a Killing-strategy Adaptive Beluga Whale Optimization (KABWO) algorithm is proposed. A thermodynamic parameter inversion framework for arch dam concrete is established. KABWO introduces an exploration-exploitation balance factor, dynamic threshold selection, and a whale-killing strategy. Twelve benchmark functions show faster convergence and higher accuracy than seven representative algorithms. A southwest arch dam is selected as a case study. Inverted parameters agree well with measured temperatures. The maximum deviation is 0.96 °C. After transfer to adjacent dam blocks, the prediction error remains within 1.17 °C, confirming transferability. The ultimate adiabatic temperature rise is about 1.5 °C lower than the laboratory value, mainly due to water–binder ratio and field conditions. For creep parameter inversion, the derived expression is consistent with experimental fitting results. The simulated strain shows closer agreement with measured data, leading to improved accuracy.

Abstract Dams are vital infrastructure for water resource management, flood control and hydropower generation, yet their long-term safety is increasingly challenged by aging structures and limited monitoring practices. As-built building information modeling (BIM) provides precise digital representations of existing conditions and supports life cycle management. However, conventional BIM pipelines, largely developed for buildings and standardized infrastructure, are not well-suited to hydraulic structures with highly customized geometries such as arch dams. To address this limitation, an Industry Foundation Class (IFC)-compliant BIM approach for geometric modeling of arch dam bodies using point cloud data is proposed. First, IFC-compliant templates are primarily designed for dam bodies, enabling standardized and expressive digital modeling of dam structures. A reconstruction pipeline is then proposed for geometric modeling of the dam body from unstructured point cloud data, integrating semantic segmentation with parametric geometric modeling techniques. The effectiveness of the proposed pipeline is demonstrated through a case study on a masonry arch dam, where point clouds captured by mobile laser scanning are processed to generate IFC-compliant BIM models. Results indicated that the method enables accurate reconstruction of complex dam geometries while ensuring interoperability within the BIM environment.

Seepage along construction joints can threaten the uplift stability and long-term safety of concrete dams. Although seepage-induced joint opening has been studied, the post-initiation transition from stable seepage to rapid uplift instability remains insufficiently understood. This study presents a coupled hydro-mechanical numerical framework with interfacial damage output to simulate the post-initiation uplift instability of concrete dam construction joints. The framework integrates hydraulic-head buildup, uplift separation, mechanically evaluated aperture evolution, interfacial damage analysis, and a seepage-velocity growth indicator. The results show that hydraulic head concentrates near the construction joint under anti-seepage constraint, reducing the effective normal stress and driving localized hydraulic separation. Uplift deformation develops near the jointed interface rather than as a uniform block deformation. Increasing the initial opening amplifies monitored uplift displacement and advances the transition from stable response to rapid separation and instability; the 3 mm opening loses stability earliest, followed by the 2 mm and 1 mm openings. The observed localization of interfacial degradation supports a damage-informed aperture interpretation in which interface deterioration may contribute to hydraulic-path development beyond mechanical opening alone. The magnitude of this additional contribution was not quantified because the damage-aperture coefficient was not independently calibrated. The normalized seepage-velocity response and velocity growth indicator further suggest that hydraulic acceleration may provide an early warning indicator of aperture-sensitive instability. These findings indicate that seepage-induced instability of dam construction joints should be evaluated through the combined evolution of hydraulic head, uplift separation, mechanically evaluated aperture, damage localization, and seepage-velocity, rather than through crack-opening initiation or displacement response alone. The proposed mechanism provides a basis for uplift instability assessment and monitoring of jointed hydraulic concrete structures.

The monitoring of the dynamic behaviour of concrete dams is an important aspect in their safety evaluation. Dynamic properties (i.e. mode shapes and natural frequencies) provide useful information on the operational behaviour of dams. In this study, the influence of the curvature (single or double), valley characteristics (narrow or wide, U or V) and classification of arch dams (thin, medium-thick and thick) on the dynamic behaviour of these dams was investigated through numerical models. The mode shape sequence was not affected by the curvature, however it was affected by the system stiffness and added mass (water level) for some configurations. The natural frequencies were generally higher for double curvature arch dams, than single curvature arch dams. The first mode shape for all V-shaped valley types was a symmetric mode followed by an antisymmetric mode. Whilst for the U-shaped valley types, the first and second mode varied between symmetric and anti-symmetric modes for different arch classifications. Based on the observations presented in this paper, the site shape, arch type, arch thickness class influence the dynamic behaviour of concrete arch dams together with the stiffness and water level. An accurate representation of these parameters is critical when performing dynamic analysis of these structures.

Advances in data science have enabled the large-scale acquisition of structural information in large dams through modern monitoring systems, fostering the development of predictive models, analytical platforms, and advanced visualization tools that provide increasingly detailed diagnostics of structural behavior. Nevertheless, despite this high level of technical sophistication, a critical limitation persists: the difficulty of translating complex analytical outputs—such as time series, dashboards, and multivariate indicators—into information that is clear, relevant, and actionable for operational and strategic decision-making. This paper contends that the primary constraint on the effectiveness of data-driven initiatives in Structural Health Monitoring is not technical but human, arising from a persistent communication gap between data analysts and structural safety managers that hinders the transformation of analytical results into consistent and timely decisions. Consequently, the interpretation of monitoring outputs often remains subjective, weakly standardized, and highly dependent on individual expertise, potentially undermining the reliability of operational responses. Drawing on recent studies and practical evidence from dam monitoring, this work analyzes the underlying causes and manifestations of this gap, evaluates its implications for structural safety, and proposes a set of mitigation strategies, including the standardization of technical language, the development of interdisiplinary skill profiles, the redesign of decision-oriented visualizations, and the implementation of protocols that explicitly connect analytical outcomes with defined operational actions.

Introduction Roller compacted concrete (RCC) is widely used in large-scale hydraulic structures, but its high heat of hydration and poor heat dissipation can easily cause temperature cracks, posing a threat to engineering safety. Traditional temperature control measures mainly focus on post-event cooling, which are passive, single and have limited effects. There is also a lack of systematic coupling of the inherent thermal properties of materials and the dynamic construction process. Therefore, this paper conducted a model test for the optimization of full-process temperature control and crack prevention, aiming to suppress the generation of temperature cracks at the source and provide a reference for the temperature control and crack prevention design and construction of RCC in water conservancy projects. Methods This paper used a 1:40 geometrically scaled block model to simulate the large-volume RCC structure of an actual gravity dam and made a similarity analysis on from aspects of geometry, hydration heat, temperature, cooling aging, stress, and cracking behavior. A reference group (G0), five single-factor optimization groups (G1 mix proportion optimization condition, G2 mixing temperature control condition, G3 pouring technique condition, G4 internal cooling condition, G5 post-curing condition), and one full-process integrated optimization group (G6) were set up. Five specimens were prepared for each group. The pouring and curing process was carried out in an environmental chamber under summer conditions. Temperature and stress data from 0 to 40 days were collected using pre-installed T-type thermocouples and vibrating wire strain gauges. Images of the surface cracks of the specimens were captured using an industrial camera and quantitatively analyzed. The evaluation indicators included maximum center temperature, maximum internal and external temperature difference, cooling rate, first crack time, total crack area, maximum crack width, maximum tensile stress, occurrence time, stress reserve coefficient. Results Each single optimization measure could reduce temperature rise, decrease temperature difference, and delay cracking to varying degrees, but the paths and magnitudes of their effects were different. G2 had a remarkable effect in reducing the peak internal temperature; G3 performed excellently in reducing temperature difference and delaying cracking; G4 had a fast cooling rate but was prone to generating secondary temperature differences, and using it alone limited anti-cracking effect; G5 had the least effect on temperature control and crack prevention. G6 had the best effect, with the peak temperature in the center being 15.4 °C lower than G0, the maximum internal and external temperature difference being only 15.1 °C, the maximum tensile stress being only 0.98 MPa, and the stress reserve coefficient reaching 1.43. No cracking occurred within the 40-day observation period. Discussion The internal temperature rise of RCC is caused by the exothermic hydration reaction of cement and fly ash. Different optimization measures have fundamentally different paths for suppressing the hydration heat. The single-factor optimization group can only address the shortcomings of a single temperature control link and cannot simultaneously meet the control conditions of low temperature rise, small gradient, slow cooling, and low stress; the full-process integrated optimization G6 forms a closed-loop temperature control system through the collaborative effect of various temperature control measures to achieve the optimal effect of no cracking within 40 days. The research results can provide references for material ratio, layered pouring, water supply cooling, and intelligent monitoring in the construction of gravity dams made of RCC.

Ensuring the seismic safety of ageing earthfill reservoir dams in tectonically active regions requires methods that link field monitoring directly to quantitative structural assessment. Existing studies, however, typically treat satellite deformation monitoring and dynamic structural modeling as separate activities. This study addresses that gap by developing an integrated framework that combines a national electronic seismic-monitoring platform, real-time instrumental accelerograms, and multi-year Sentinel-1 satellite radar interferometry (InSAR) within a single, traceable chain of analytical and finite-element models. The framework is applicable to both near-field and far-field earthquakes; here it is applied to the earthfill Surkhan reservoir dam (Uzbekistan) following the strong far-field earthquake that occurred in Afghanistan on 3 November 2025 ( M = 6.8, h = 30 km). Seven years of InSAR data (2017-2023) show that the dam deformation is predominantly seasonal, governed by the reservoir loading cycle, with point-wise cumulative trends that require continued monitoring, while the instrumental records show that the earthquake added only a sub-millimeter transient response well within the elastic range. The macroseismic intensity prediction agrees closely with the instrumental observation, whereas the free-field ground-motion model under-predicts the recorded acceleration by more than an order of magnitude, possible explanations include local site and crest amplification, sensor position and processing, and event-specific source effects, and these remain to be examined against the raw records; the observed site intensity (5 MSK-64) was two intensity degrees below the design-basis intensity of the dam (7 MSK-64). The novelty of the work lies in the joint interpretation of long-term satellite and short-term seismic datasets through one traceable model chain, partially checked against the monitored intensity and displacement quantities, yielding a low-cost, replicable methodology for the rapid post-earthquake safety assessment of reservoir dams in seismically active regions.

Drainage is widely recognized, both in geotechnical literature and in mining engineering practice, as one of the determining factors for the stability of earth structures built with or composed of mining waste materials. This technical article addresses the research problem of identifying the influence of surface and deep drainage systems on the stability and operational safety of mining geotechnical structures, particularly pit and stack slopes, waste rock piles and tailings disposal structures (dams and dry-stacked or filtered tailings piles). Through a narrative review of technical and regulatory literature, an analysis of soil mechanics principles applied to pore pressure and shear strength, and the update of a comparative study of deep drainage alternatives originally developed in an undergraduate thesis, the article discusses the main failure mechanisms associated with saturation and positive pore pressure generation, the types of surface and deep drainage devices available, their design criteria and good practices for design, construction, operation and monitoring. Four typical deep drainage alternatives — horizontal drains, relief wells, drainage blankets and vertical drainage trenches — are compared according to design flow rate, safety level provided, implementation cost and execution schedule, showing that the optimal solution depends on the geological-geotechnical context, the stage of the work and the risk appetite of the project. Results indicate that efficient drainage reduces pore pressures, increases the factor of safety against shear failure, decreases the probability of liquefaction in saturated tailings, and constitutes, together with geotechnical instrumentation, one of the pillars of dam and waste pile safety management systems in Brazil, especially after the Fundão (Mariana/MG, 2015) and Córrego do Feijão Mine (Brumadinho/MG, 2019) disasters, which reshaped the national regulatory framework. It is concluded that drainage should not be treated as an accessory design element, but as a structural safety component, subject to formal design, redundancy, periodic inspection and instrumented monitoring throughout the entire life cycle of the mining project.

The inspection of concrete structures, including bridges, buildings, and dams, is vital for ensuring public safety and infrastructure longevity. Traditional methods, relying heavily on manual labor and rudimentary tools, are time-intensive, prone to human error, and often expose inspectors to hazardous conditions. To overcome these challenges, this thesis presents an autonomous mobile robot (AMR) system integrating advanced navigation, precise data acquisition, defect detection, and crack analysis capabilities. Equipped with multiple cameras for high-resolution imaging and depth sensing, the robot employs Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) techniques for accurate navigation and environmental mapping. Captured data undergo preprocessing, including noise reduction and contrast enhancement, followed by crack detection and segmentation using YOLOv8. The system automatically records the location of defects and analyzes each by measuring crack lengths and widths through pixel-to-metric conversions using calibrated camera parameters. The proposed robotic approach significantly enhances inspection accuracy, efficiency, and safety, representing a transformative solution for continuous structural health monitoring

Dam-safety assessment requires integrated interpretation of numerical outputs and field monitoring while recognizing whether the compared observations represent equivalent flow domains. This study evaluates seepage at Raknamo Dam for two reservoir states, 99.68 and 104.18 m above sea level, together with slope stability under static, Operating Basis Earthquake (OBE), Maximum Design Earthquake (MDE), and rapid-drawdown conditions. SEEP/W yielded unit-width discharges of 3.0587×10⁻⁶ and 4.2983×10⁻⁶ m³/s/m. Scaling by the dam length produced section-equivalent values of 0.001376 and 0.001933 m³/s, whereas V-notch monitoring recorded 0.00360 and 0.00992 m³/s. Because longitudinal uniformity and equivalence between the modeled section and the V-notch catchment cannot be demonstrated, these quantities are not treated as equivalent observations for model validation or error estimation. V-notch data are therefore reported as independent operational monitoring evidence alongside the numerical outputs. SLOPE/W safety factors ranged from 2.082–2.504 under static conditions, 1.888–2.068 under OBE, and 1.257–1.400 under MDE. The two upstream MDE results, 1.259 at 99.68 m and 1.257 at 104.18 m, are considered practically indistinguishable at the available reporting precision because no sensitivity or uncertainty analysis was performed. The final rapid-drawdown condition after 18 h yielded a safety factor of 2.417, while the minimum factor of safety during the transient history is unavailable. The study demonstrates the value of complementary, but explicitly non-equivalent, monitoring and modeling evidence and clarifies the inference limits imposed by incomplete monitoring metadata and archived numerical-model information.

Unowned low-height earth dams, whose safety level is different from normal and low, are a source of increased danger, as the condition of these structures is not monitored, and structural defects that occur over time are not detected or repaired in a timely manner. The inventory of low-pressure earth dams located in the Moscow region provided data from a one-time expert survey of these structures. Using machine learning methods, an express model of probabilistic forecast of the safety level of low-head homogeneous earth dams has been developed, linking the probability of the dam compliance with the normal or reduced safety level not only with the age of the structure, but also with the maximum height along the crest, the presence of the upper slope fastening and the road on the dam crest. The model is suitable for forecasting the safety level of unowned earth dams located in the Moscow region. The research results can be directly applied by dam owners or municipal executive authorities when planning the repair dates of unowned dams.

Structural operational safety assessment of high concrete arch dams remains challenging because the importance of monitoring indicators varies with operating conditions, while the evaluation process is affected by multiple sources of uncertainty. To address these issues, this study develops a dynamic data-driven evaluation framework for structural operational safety assessment. Initially, a hierarchical indicator system and a refined grading scheme are established using multi-source structural response sequences. An adaptive weighting mechanism is then developed by coupling the cross-correlation function with Apriori-based association rule mining, enabling indicator weights to be dynamically updated according to the correlation and association characteristics between reservoir water-level variations and structural responses. Furthermore, Interval-Valued Intuitionistic Fuzzy Sets (IVIFSs) are introduced to explicitly represent membership, non-membership and hesitation information, allowing randomness, fuzziness, and expert cognitive uncertainty to be jointly characterized within a unified reasoning framework. The proposed method is validated using monitoring data from the Jinping-I arch dam. Comparative results demonstrate that it provides more stable and discriminative safety-state assessment than conventional static-weight and fuzzy evaluation approaches, while retaining greater adaptability to time-varying structural behavior. The framework further transforms heterogeneous monitoring information into interpretable safety states and spatially explicit diagnostic information, providing a practical basis for real-time safety assessment, targeted inspection and intelligent operation and maintenance of high arch dams.

Background: Environmental pollution from heavy metals poses a global public health concern, especially in developing countries with intensive mining and poor waste management. In Zimbabwe, freshwater bodies such as Ngamo Dam are at risk of contamination, affecting aquatic organisms and human consumers. This study aimed to investigate the levels of cadmium (Cd), copper (Cu), lead (Pb), manganese (Mn), and zinc (Zn) in Oreochromis niloticus (O. niloticus) and water samples from Ngamo Dam to assess their safety for human consumption. Methods: Water and fish samples were collected from three sites in Ngamo Dam between January and February 2024. Fish gills and muscles were prepared using wet acid digestion, while water samples were digested with nitric acid. Metal concentrations were analyzed using Atomic Absorption Spectrophotometry (AAS). Statistical analysis was performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test to determine significant differences among sampling sites (p < 0.05). Results: Water samples showed heavy metal concentrations exceeding World Health Organization (WHO) and Standards Association of Zimbabwe (SAZ) permissible limits: Pb (5.21–10.30 mg/L), Cu (5.67–8.56 mg/L), Mn (2.96–4.34 mg/L), Zn (2.15–3.67 mg/L), and Cd (1.34–3.23 mg/L). In O. niloticus gills, the order of accumulation was Cu > Zn > Pb > Cd > Mn, with Cu reaching 11.44 mg/kg. Muscles showed lower but significant accumulation, with Cu (5.87–12.62 mg/kg) and Pb (1.39–4.19 mg/kg) being prominent. Pb levels in water exceeded WHO limits by up to 10 times, while Cd exceeded permissible limits by approximately 6 times. Both water and fish samples contained heavy metal concentrations above recommended safety thresholds. A summary of all concentrations is provided in Table 1. Conclusion: The findings reveal high levels of heavy metal bioaccumulation in Ngamo Dam water and fish, rendering them unsafe for human consumption. Continuous monitoring, implementation of remediation strategies, and strict regulation of anthropogenic activities around the dam are necessary to protect public and ecological health. Authorities should consider bioremediation and improved waste management practices to reduce contamination.

Fish serve as a vital, affordable source of animal protein in Nigeria, but parasitic infections and environmental degradation threaten the sustainability of aquaculture. This study evaluated parasitic infections, water quality, and organ histopathology in wild (n = 174; catfish and tilapia) and cultured (n = 150; catfish) fish across Jos Metropolis, Plateau State, during the 2025 rainy season (May–October). Physicochemical water parameters generally met standard aquaculture guidelines across all sites. However, cultured environments showed higher nutrient enrichment, featuring elevated turbidity (10.5-12.6 NTU), conductivity (181-190 μS/cm), nitrate (6.2–7.5 mg/L), and phosphate (0.54-0.61 mg/L). Overall prevalence rates for haemoparasites and intestinal parasites were 24.1 % (78/324) and 15.7 % (51/324), respectively. Haemoparasite (Haemogregarina spp.) prevalence was significantly higher in wild fish, peaking at 87.5 % in Oreochromis niloticus from Kara Dam, compared to 0.0-30.0 % in cultured catfish. In contrast, intestinal parasite rates were similar between wild (15.5 %) and cultured fish (16.0 %), with Entamoeba spp. identified as the predominant taxon. Histopathological evaluation demonstrated more severe hepatic and renal lesions—primarily congestion and focal necrosis—in wild fish, aligning with their elevated haemoparasite burden. Cultured fish displayed milder pathological alterations despite facing higher nutrient loads, while gastric tissues showed no significant damage across groups. Overall, these findings demonstrate that wild fish face greater parasite-induced pathology, whereas cultured systems show elevated nutrient levels. Implementing routine parasitological monitoring, proactive aquaculture management, and improved environmental sanitation is essential to safeguard fish health, ensure food security, and protect public safety in the region.

Penguatan kompetensi pengelola bendungan diperlukan untuk menjaga keselamatan struktur, efektivitas operasi, dan kualitas pengambilan keputusan. Kajian ini merumuskan strategi peningkatan kompetensi yang terintegrasi melalui tiga pilar: pelatihan berkelanjutan berbasis kompetensi, mekanisme transfer pengetahuan yang sistematis, dan teknologi pemantauan terintegrasi. Penelitian menggunakan desain kualitatif-deskriptif dengan literature review, telaah kebijakan/pedoman teknis, serta interpretasi temuan observasi untuk memetakan kebutuhan dan hambatan peningkatan kompetensi. Hasil analisis menunjukkan kebutuhan kompetensi inti mencakup teknis-operasional, manajerial, mitigasi risiko, dan literasi teknologi. Strategi yang diusulkan memperluas akses pembelajaran dan mendukung pengelolaan bendungan berbasis data untuk mendukung ketahanan air, pangan, dan energi. Competency strengthening for dam management personnel is essential to safeguard structural safety, enhance operational effectiveness, and improve the quality of decision-making. This study formulates an integrated competency development strategy built on three pillars: competency-based continuous training, systematic knowledge-transfer mechanisms, and integrated monitoring technologies. The research adopts a qualitative descriptive design, employing a literature review, an examination of relevant policies and technical guidelines, and the interpretation of observational findings to map competency needs and key barriers to competency improvement. The analysis indicates that core competency requirements involve technical–operational, managerial, risk-mitigation, and technological literacy domains. The proposed strategy broadens access to learning and supports data-driven dam management to strengthen national water, food, and energy security.

Abstract The safety of long-standing concrete dams still in operation is based on the analysis of data provided by accurate monitoring systems. Periodic measurements are performed by sensors positioned at specific sensitive locations such as the crest of the dam, or inside its body. Models of the structural behaviour support the interpretation of the information thus collected. Data-driven approaches based on machine-learning algorithms are often used. Once properly trained and tested, these techniques are effective in detecting anomalies in the structural response, possibly due to ongoing damage processes. The reliability of the outcomes provided by these potential warning systems can be significantly increased by integrating data-driven methods with physics-based simulation models. The realism and accuracy of the latter depend on the availability of displacement and temperature distributions over large portions of the exposed surfaces of the dam under study. These measurements can be provided by non-contact infrared and vision-based techniques, which are currently widely available. However, variations due to degradation processes may be low, and can be confused with experimental errors. Future advances in sensor technology are expected to improve measurement accuracy, while the integration of different sensing techniques could enhance the detectability and interpretation of even subtle changes.

Civil engineering structures such as high-rise buildings, bridges, dams, etc. are critical systems in every society. Such structures are exposed to non-destructive and destructive loads and vibrations such as earthquakes during their operations. Moreover, aging and material deterioration of some structures that have been several years ago will affect the structural performance and integrity. To prevent damage and its adverse effects, structural health monitoring (SHM) is of a paramount importance to civil engineering communities. The main objective of SHM is to assess the safety and integrity of civil structures to understand their current conditions and detect any possible damage due to changes in dynamic characteristics. To implement an SHM strategy, it is possible to utilize two methods; that is, model-based and data-based approaches. The former is based on modeling of an accurate finite element model of the real structure and applying the theory of model updating for SHM. In contrast, the latter only uses raw measured data such as acceleration time histories under the theory of statistical pattern recognition. Having considered the disadvantages and advantages of each of the mentioned SHM approaches, the main aim of this dissertation is to propose new and practical methods in both aspects of the model-based data-based algorithms. In the first part, one attempts to detect damage in bridge structures with different boundary conditions using the structural energy and the Riley-Ritz method. In this regard, the limitations of the Ritz method are dealt with by proposing various functions, adding a penalty parameter, and developing the governing relationships. One of the advantages of the improved Ritz method is that its generality for implementing on a broad range of bridge structures using modal data. Results of this part of dissertation will demonstrate that the improved Ritz method is able to detect damage in multi-span continuous bridges with lateral displacements. In the second part, the process of health monitoring in civil structures is studied by the concept of data-based approach with the focus on addressing the limitation of applying high-dimensional data. On this basis, one of the important objectives of this dissertation in this part is to propose practical and new methods to reduce the volume of data by about 0.1% of the initial data for damage detection. In the first proposed method, the relative norm error of the residuals of time series models called the residual relative error (RRE) and Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) is presented to reduce the dimension of data. In the following, the well-known Mahalanobis distance and a threshold limit are applied to detect, locate, and quantify damage in two benchmark structures. The second data-based method proposes two hybrid algorithms by reducing the size of features. Each of the proposed methods consists of a three-stage algorithm including response modelling via a time series representation, Gaussian mixture model (GMM) for dimensionality reduction, and an outlier detector. Due to the importance of response modelling under ambient vibration, these algorithms employ the combination of AR with ARX called the ARARX model. In the second stage, a GMM is individually fitted to residual samples extracted from ARARX regarding the undamaged and damaged conditions to obtain low-dimensional features from massive data. Eventually, outlier analyses are carried out by the Mahalanobis distance and an auto-associative neural network to make a decision about the occurrence of damage. A large-scale cable-stayed bridge is applied to validate the reliability and effectiveness of these algorithms.

Accurate deformation prediction of high arch dams is essential for ensuring long-term structural safety and operational reliability. However, conventional deformation models are predominantly developed based on individual monitoring points, which neglect the spatial correlations embedded in dam monitoring networks. Moreover, the predictive performance of these models is highly dependent on the selection of informative influencing factors, limiting their generalization capability under complex operating conditions. To address these limitations, this study proposes an entropy-guided multi-point deformation prediction framework for high arch dams that integrates Copula Entropy-based feature selection with an optimized inverted Transformer (iTransformer) model. First, the influence of near-dam mountain mass on dam deformation is explicitly considered, and mountain-enhanced hydrostatic-seasonal-time (MHST) factors are constructed using near-dam mountain residuals after least-squares removal of conventional hydrostatic, seasonal, and time-dependent components. Subsequently, a Copula Entropy-based partial mutual information (PMI) strategy is developed to quantify nonlinear dependencies between candidate influencing factors and multi-point deformation responses, enabling the construction of a compact and low-redundancy feature set. Furthermore, an iTransformer-based multi-output prediction model is established to capture spatially coordinated deformation patterns among multiple monitoring locations. An artificial ecosystem-based optimization algorithm (AEO) is introduced to optimize model hyperparameters and improve prediction robustness. The proposed framework enables synchronous deformation prediction across multiple monitoring points using physically interpretable input factors. Long-term field monitoring data from a large-scale high arch dam are employed to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Results demonstrate that the proposed model attains the lowest average root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.043 among the compared learning-based models. Although point-specific factor selection performs slightly better at TCN10 and TCN11, the proposed model provides the best aggregate performance across the three monitoring points, indicating its potential for dam health monitoring and safety assessment.

Automated safety interpretation of concrete-dam cracks remains challenging because crack-gauge records may be incomplete, abnormal changes are difficult to distinguish from normal evolution, and monitoring outputs are not readily translated into traceable decisions. This paper proposes a mutation-aware visual–sensor fusion and knowledge-augmented framework. A deep learning model, multiscale dynamic spatial YOLOv11n (MDS-YOLOv11n), extracts crack widths from images and aligns them with crack-gauge measurements to supplement missing observations. Autoformer models the fused sequence; a dynamic three-sigma (3 σ ) criterion identifies persistent deviations, and a Heaviside–exponential moving average (EMA) reconstructs mutation-induced increments. Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) connects mutation-analysis outputs with dam-crack safety knowledge. Validation on a concrete dam showed better prediction performance than comparative models; GraphRAG produced recommendations for intensified monitoring and sensor inspection, consistent with periodic inspection records. The framework establishes an automated pathway from multimodal physical observation to crack-state interpretation and knowledge-driven decision support for operation and maintenance.

The Mw 7.7 Myanmar earthquake of 28 March 2025 generated ground shaking across several regions of Thailand, including Nakhon Ratchasima Province, where the Lam Chae Earth Dam is located. Rapid and reliable assessment of dam stability following seismic events is essential for ensuring public safety and supporting reservoir operation. In this context, Sentinel-1 Differential Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (DInSAR) provides spatially continuous deformation measurements over large areas and complements conventional point-based field monitoring instruments. This study presents an integrated assessment of earthquake-induced dam stability using Sentinel-1 DInSAR together with field instrumentation, including inclinometers and piezometers. Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images acquired during the pre-seismic, co-seismic, and post-seismic periods were processed to derive line-of-sight (LOS) surface deformation and compared with in-situ monitoring data. The DInSAR analysis revealed a maximum cumulative LOS displacement ranging from approximately - 27 to - 30 mm during the co-seismic period, whereas inclinometer measurements indicated internal deformation ranging from - 1.258 to - 3.980 mm. Piezometer observations confirmed that pore-water pressure remained within the normal operating range throughout the monitoring period. Although DInSAR measurements are subject to uncertainties associated with atmospheric delay, temporal decorrelation, and vegetation-induced coherence loss, the observed deformation patterns were consistent with field measurements, providing complementary evidence for assessing dam behaviour. This study demonstrates the applicability of integrating satellite-based DInSAR with conventional geotechnical instrumentation for post-earthquake dam safety assessment in Thailand, where such integrated applications remain limited. The integrated interpretation of satellite- and ground-based monitoring indicates that the Lam Chae Earth Dam remained structurally stable following the earthquake and provides a practical framework for long-term structural health monitoring of earth dams.

Concrete-face rockfill dams (CFRDs) constructed in narrow valleys and on spatially heterogeneous foundations may experience nonuniform seepage and deformation, while local defects in the seepage-control system can further affect their operational safety. This study establishes a three-dimensional finite element model of the 90 m-high Yecha CFRD to systematically evaluate seepage behavior, stress–deformation response, face slab performance, and slope stability under normal, extreme-water-level, and representative defect scenarios. The seepage analysis considers different reservoir levels as well as peripheral-joint failure, face slab cracking at different elevations, and grout-curtain degradation, while the nonlinear mechanical behavior of the rockfill is described using the Duncan–Chang E–B model with parameters obtained from large-scale triaxial tests. Under normal storage, the seepage-control system remains effective, with a total seepage discharge of 3240.18 m3/d. The maximum dam settlement is 25.15 cm, corresponding to 0.279% of the dam height, and the slope safety factor is 1.48. Low-elevation face slab cracking is identified as a critical local seepage scenario, increasing the hydraulic gradient in the cushion material to 3.39, above the allowable value of 0.45. In addition, a 20% reduction in the mechanical parameters of the main rockfill zones increases the maximum settlement and face slab deflection by 84% and 74%, respectively, indicating a pronounced sensitivity to rockfill mechanical properties. Under the check flood level, the minimum slope safety factor decreases to 1.39 but remains above the code requirement. These results highlight low-elevation face slab integrity and rockfill compaction quality as key factors governing the seepage and deformation safety of CFRDs and provide a practical basis for defect-oriented monitoring and safety assessment.

Automated dam-safety monitoring compares each pendulum reading with a prediction band from data-driven predictive models, but its operational deployment is undermined by alarm fatigue: because prediction residuals are autocorrelated, band transgressions might arrive in clustered streaks and a per-record threshold overwhelms the operator with redundant warnings. This work treats the transgressions as a binary time series whose normal behaviour is learned during training and compares three detectors, each addressing a limitation of the previous one: a Gaussian-threshold baseline (M0), a sliding-window detector with a 99th-percentile threshold whose window is sized from the residual autocorrelation (P99), and a two-state hidden Markov model (HMM) that learns the persistence of the streaks. Applied to 28 pendulums of three dams, M0 can even increase the number of flagged records, whereas the HMM flags the fewest: in the largest case study it reduces them by 58.960 % with respect to the raw transgression series and by 45.594 % with respect to P99. An identifiability criterion based on the emission separation indicates when the HMM can be trusted (20 of 28 sensors) and when to fall back to P99, and a sensitivity analysis shows that the estimates are robust in a neighbourhood of the reference initialisation, with the self-transition probability of the Normal state as the critical parameter.

Ground-based radar (GBR) monitoring uses microwave radar to remotely measure ground and structural movements with millimeter-scale precision. Its objectives are to provide continuous, high-frequency deformation data for slopes, mines, dams, and other geohazards, improving safety and risk management. Key radar types include real-aperture pulse/FMCW systems (e.g., IBIS-S), synthetic aperture radar (SAR) interferometry (millimeter-wave, e.g., IBIS-FM/SSR), and ground-penetrating radar (GPR). This chapter presents an in-depth technical overview: operating principles of interferometric radars, sweep radars, and GPR; system components (antennas, transmit/receive hardware, interferometers, and processing units); and measurement geometry (LOS, pixel size, and baseline considerations). Performance parameters (accuracy, resolution, and range) and limitations (atmosphere, layover, and multipath) are also discussed. We describe data processing (phase unwrapping, coherence filtering, atmospheric correction) and data fusion with LiDAR/Prisms/GNSS/InSAR. Deployment methods (fixed tripod, gantry, vehicle, and UAV) and planning guidelines are given. Two worked examples (converting phase change to displacement; range resolution vs bandwidth) with equations illustrate system design. We include comparison tables of radar system attributes (range, resolution, and cost/complexity) and deployment checklists. Case studies (e.g., open-pit slope, tailings dam, and tunnel) illustrate successes and failures of radar monitoring. This chapter also addresses digital integration (IoT telemetry, real-time processing, and digital twins) and define alarm frameworks using radar data. Throughout, we cite recent reviews and standards to guide robust GBR monitoring practice.

Geotechnical monitoring is the systematic measurement of ground and structure behavior displacements, pressures, etc. to ensure the safety and performance of mining and civil works. Its core objectives are safety (early warning of instability) and design validation (verifying model predictions), enabling timely interventions or design optimizations. Historically, major failures, notably the 2019 Brumadinho tailings dam collapse (272 fatalities), have underscored the need for rigorous monitoring. In response, industry standards (ICMM’s tailings standard and guidelines) now mandate continuous monitoring (with zero tolerance for human fatality and the ultimate goal of zero harm). This chapter reviews the principles, instrumentation, and methods of modern geotechnical monitoring in mining. It covers planning and design of monitoring programs (OMS manuals, failure modes, redundancy), a survey of sensor types (borehole gauges, inclinometers, piezometers, tiltmeters, extensometers, surveying, InSAR, UAV, and ground-based remote sensing) with a comparison table of their attributes, and data acquisition/quality approaches (telemetry, calibration, maintenance). Basic analytics (trend analysis, alarms, thresholds, decision frameworks, and AI caveats) are discussed, along with the integration of monitoring into the Mining 4.0 paradigm (IoT networks, real-time dashboards, digital twins). Representative case studies illustrate these concepts: for example, satellite InSAR detected pre-failure slope movements in Brazilian open pits. An automated prism/radar network in an Australian mine enabled continuous wall surveillance, and a New Zealand mine implemented a 3D digital twin for its tailings dam to fuse real-time sensor data and models. Finally, common challenges and best practices (avoiding data overload, ensuring data reliability, cross-checking signals, etc.) are summarized. Throughout, emphasis is on a comprehensive, industry-focused presentation with up-to-date references to standards and recent research.

In-ground monitoring involves installing sensors in boreholes and within soil or rock masses to measure subsurface behavior critical for mining safety and design validation. Key objectives are to detect movements or stresses below ground, verify geotechnical models, and provide early warning of instability. This chapter covers the range of in-ground instruments (inclinometers, extensometers, piezometers, pressure cells, strain gauges, distributed fiber-optic sensing, tiltmeters, settlement plates, and seismic/acoustic sensors), their installation practices (borehole drilling, casing, and grouting), and best practices. We present sensor selection criteria and comparison tables that show measurement ranges, accuracy, and relative complexities. Two worked examples illustrate borehole network design and corrections (e.g., inclinometer spacing and barometric correction of piezometers). Data acquisition and quality control methods are discussed (telemetry, calibration, and filtering), along with interpretation basics (time-series analysis, trend detection, and noise handling). Guidance on alarm thresholds and decision frameworks (TARPs) specific to in-ground data is provided. We include a mermaid diagram of typical data flow architecture, and at least three case studies (tailings dam, slope, and underground), highlighting lessons learned. Tables present pre-installation and commissioning checklists for field teams. Recommendations emphasize Mining 4.0 integration (IoT, real-time dashboards, and digital twins) and cite recent standards (e.g., GISTM and OMS guidelines).

ABSTRACT In the digital transformation era, civil engineering infrastructure is undergoing profound life-cycle evolution, enhancing efficiency, safety, sustainability, and resilience. Given their unique nature and the complexity of their design, construction, and management, as well as their direct impact on water security and public safety, Hydropower and Dam Structures (HDS) are a high-priority domain for the implementation of digital technologies, particularly Building Information Modeling (BIM), the Internet of Things, and artificial intelligence. This paper aims to provide an in-depth state-of-the-art review of the implementation of digital technologies, particularly BIM and Digital Twin, in HDS, with a focus on real-time Structural Health Monitoring (SHM). This review builds on a systematic and critical analysis of more than 120 carefully selected, highly relevant references. It investigates the main digital technologies supporting HDS transformation (information modeling, data acquisition and pipelines, and data processing) and highlights adoption drivers and barriers in developed and developing countries. It clarifies the concepts of BIM and Digital Twin, along with the supporting tools and technologies. It also summarizes the most recent life-cycle HDS applications and discusses interoperability challenges and potential solutions. In particular, the review provides further insights into real-time SHM of HDS by analyzing the most advanced BIM-driven case studies integrating the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, numerical simulations, and remote sensing. This review establishes a comprehensive foundation and provides practical recommendations to guide researchers and practitioners seeking to design, assess, and operationalize digital solutions for large civil infrastructure, thereby accelerating digital transformation while strengthening safety, intelligence, and resilience.

Civil structures and infrastructures, such as bridges, high-rise buildings, towers, dams, tunnels, and so forth, occupy a major position in the economy and play a vital role in facilitating daily life for the world population. However, accidental structural damage can cause significant economic and human casualties. Thus, structural health monitoring is necessary for the longevity of the building and the safety of the public. Structural health monitoring is the process of implementing a damage detection and characterization strategy for engineering structures. Structural health monitoring pertains to the life of a structure and diagnoses the ‘‘state” of the constituted materials in different parts of the structure. Recent advances in monitoring systems, sensor technologies, and artificial intelligence have promoted the integration of multi-source data and the adoption of intelligent algorithms, positioning structural health monitoring (SHM) at the forefront of addressing these challenges. By synthesizing advanced sensing, numerical simulation, and machine learning, SHM systems establish an intelligent feedback loop of sensing–diagnosis–prediction, substantially improving monitoring efficacy and proactive maintenance. This Reprint is dedicated to presenting the latest research progress in civil structural health monitoring, encompassing areas such as damage detection, data processing algorithms, modeling and simulation, sensor development, and experimental validation.

Structural dam safety control is fundamentally based on visual inspections and on the analysis of monitoring data and their comparison with the expected behavior for a given load combination, which in turn is calculated with a predictive model. In recent decades, the development of machine learning algorithms has led engineers and researchers worldwide to explore their capabilities for predicting dam behavior and supporting safety assessment. Regardless of the model used, a prediction is generally obtained together with an expected model error, which is compared with the observed value in order to support decision-making. This process, however, requires the intervention of experts in dam engineering, and particularly in the prior behavior of the structure under analysis. In recent years, the emergence of generative artificial intelligence models has opened up considerable opportunities to improve processes in various fields, including civil engineering. The reported capabilities of these models make them well suited to some tasks in the field of dam safety, particularly for developing predictive models and interpreting their results. In this work, we tested ChatGPT to assess its potential in these tasks, using the data from the ICOLD 2022 Benchmark Workshop, in which 18 teams provided their best predictions of the behavior of an arch dam. ChatGPT was provided with the same problem description and monitoring data available to the participants and was asked, through brief and neutral prompts, to propose a modeling strategy, generate predictions for six response variables for short- and long-term periods, create the corresponding source code, and interpret the results from a dam safety perspective. The complete procedure was performed twice using the same information and prompts. The results show considerable potential for increasing productivity in building and applying machine learning models, with predictive accuracy comparable to that obtained by the Benchmark participants. ChatGPT achieved a lower mean absolute error than the participants’ average in 10 (first run) and 12 (second run) of the 12 variable–period combinations, and outperformed the best participant in one case. However, the interpretation of the results was considerably weaker, with important aspects being only partially addressed or overlooked. These findings highlight the potential of ChatGPT to assist in the development of data-based predictive models, but also reveal its limitations in terms of the domain-specific knowledge required to draw conclusions on dam safety.

Relevance. Tailing storage facilities (TSFs) are among the most accident-prone hydraulic structures in the mining industry, with a reported average failure-rate estimate of approximately 1.2%, while independent cumulative estimates range from 1.2% to 4.4% depending on the assumed global TSF inventory—nearly 120 times higher than that of traditional large reservoir facilities. Collapse of such structures is accompanied by catastrophic environmental and socioeconomic consequences, which underscore the need to improve monitoring and early-warning systems. Goal. A systematic analysis of current technologies for monitoring deformations in ground dams of TSFs, a quantitative assessment of their capabilities and limitations, and development of a conceptual architecture for an integrated geospatial monitoring system. Methods. A systematic review was conducted for 129 publications (2017–2026) discussing monitoring methods (GNSS, InSAR, SBAS, PS-InSAR, GB-InSAR, UAV, LiDAR, geotechnical sensors, geophysics), data integration technologies, AI/ML forecasting, digital twins, and early-warning systems. Results. It has been determined that no isolated method on its own provides complete monitoring of the structure’s condition: GNSS data are localized; InSAR loses coherence when deformations exceed 15 cm/year; UAVs are weather-dependent; and geotechnical sensors are point-based. Individual studies report reductions in estimation uncertainty of approximately 20–50% when complementary monitoring sources are integrated. Individual studies also report reductions in EWS response time and extended forecast lead times, but these values are heterogeneous and are not pooled in the present review. In one case study, a hybrid FEM–ANN–LSTM model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.027 for forecasting the dimensionless factor of safety (FoS) compared with 0.081 for an SVM baseline. Key research gaps have been identified: lack of explainable AI, limited validation of digital twins, absence of standardization in data fusion, and the lack of integration of climate risks. Conclusions. Further improvements in TSF safety require a shift from a set of independent monitoring methods to an integrated geospatial system that combines satellite, ground-based, geotechnical, and geophysical data with artificial intelligence, digital twins, and smart decision support systems. An eight-level architecture for such a system has been proposed, along with three implementation scenarios (minimal, comprehensive, and intelligent) and a roadmap through 2035.

This study presents a Digital Twin-based Structural Health Monitoring framework for the assessment of existing concrete gravity dams. The proposed methodology integrates distributed sensing, automated signal processing, finite element modelling, model calibration and validation, degradation sensitivity analysis, and digital visualization within a unified monitoring framework. A network of inertial sensors is deployed along the dam to characterize its dynamic and quasi-static response. Hourly monitoring records are processed to identify natural frequencies using Fast Fourier Transform, Power Spectral Density, and Peak Picking techniques, while acceleration measurements are also used to derive displacement and inclination indicators. A 3D finite element model developed in ANSYS Mechanical APDL is calibrated by iteratively updating the effective Young’s modulus and density until the relative error between numerical and experimentally identified modal frequencies is below 5%. Independent validation using inclination measurements resulted in relative differences between 0.74% and 4.92%. The calibrated Digital Twin is subsequently used to simulate progressive stiffness degradation and establish relationships between degradation, modal properties, and structural deformation. The resulting model-informed thresholds are integrated into a digital monitoring platform for automated condition assessment and anomaly detection. The framework provides a physically interpretable approach for complementing conventional dam safety inspections with long-term quantitative structural health information.

Introduction Extreme inflow does not necessarily raise a reservoir above its check flood level. Dam-response assessment must therefore reconcile the hydraulic boundary condition with the temporal coverage of the monitoring record. Methods We reassessed deformation, piezometric, uplift, strain, stress, and temperature observations from a 71.50 m high double-curvature concrete arch dam in southern China. Results Peak inflow was reported as 3,440 m 3 /s, above the 1,000 year reference inflow of 2,910 m 3 /s. The reservoir reached 160.29 m at 14:00 on 22 May 2025, 0.29 m above the design flood level and 0.13 m below the check flood level. Discrete surface surveys showed central radial differences of 5.65–5.99 mm between the reported survey epochs, whose exact dates were not retained. In the vertical-displacement table, +0.87 mm is the BD5 interval difference, whereas −0.15 mm belongs to BD1. Project-derived uplift coefficients at P1–P4 ranged from 0.07 to 0.21 at a reservoir level of 160.29 m. These values were 16%–72% below the project design reference of 0.25. The raw abutment-piezometric workbook contained no observations, and a plotted value of 165.28 m could not be reconciled with the dam datum. Automatic stress, strain, and temperature records generally stopped on 21 May and resumed on 8 June, leaving the flood peak unobserved. Discussion The archive consequently cannot resolve the peak response, separate thermal and hydraulic effects, test recovery, or establish a formal hydraulic threshold. The available evidence documents the event but does not establish piping, elastic recovery, or structural safety. This case highlights the need for synchronized event acquisition, verified datums, calibration metadata, and targeted inspection before diagnostic or remedial decisions are made.

Human-built infrastructure must be monitored to ensure the safety of its users. Therefore, Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) of concrete structures such as bridges, dams and tunnels is increasingly being carried out, by using automated methods rather than traditional manual methods. This study will examine data acquisition methods for developing reliable databases on cracks in concrete structures. A key focus of this study will be the major role of drones in capturing high-resolution optical and thermal images. The reliability of AI-based models depends on effective noise handling, by using techniques such as RANSAC, and adaptive binarization to adress environmental interference. By comparing field methodologies, the study looks at the trade-offs between measurement accuracy, cost, and real-time processing for future automated infrastructure assessment.

Abstract Traditional finite element methods (FEM) often exhibit insufficient accuracy and stability in stress-deformation analysis of ultra-high core rockfill dams due to element distortion and volumetric locking.
